how-much-to-charge-to-paint-the-exterior.text:
← Exterior painting bid calculator

How much to charge to paint the exterior of a house

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$3,999 house special.” That number is not a takeoff. A one-story ranch with 1,800 square feet of sound existing paint is not the same job as a two-story colonial with 2,800 square feet of elevation, 240 feet of window and fascia trim, occupied landscaping, and hard second-story access. The word “paint the house” is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the elevation and the stories, not just the special

Interior-painting calculators price rooms, walls, and ceilings. Cabinet-refinishing calculators price doors and drawers. An exterior paint job is an elevation takeoff: the included ranch, the extra story the coupon never mentions, the extra square footage of siding, and whether the existing film has to be scraped and primed. Quoting all of that from a published house special is how the first extra story eats the field margin.

A job with a similar first-story wall can cost much more

Each extra story is a taller ladder, a second-floor run, and time that never appears on the coupon. Extra elevation over the included 1,600-square-foot ranch is billed as its own hours and extra paint. Failing paint, extra trim, shutters, occupied protection, and hard access are adders that get forgotten on a ranch special. On the sample rates a 2-story 2,800 sf colonial with 240 lf of trim, twelve shutters, occupied protection, and hard access prices about $6,287 ($2.25 per elevation square foot, 62.4 crew-hours). The same shop’s 1,800 sf one-story ranch prices about $1,940 ($1.08 per square foot, 12.5 hours, walk-away $1,397). Matching a $3,999 Facebook special on the colonial is how that job becomes a loss of about $528.

A scrape-and-prime ranch is not automatically the cheap one

A 1-story 2,200 sf scrape-and-prime job with occupied landscaping is not the ranch special plus 20%. On the sample rates that scrape job prices about $8,180 ($3.72 per square foot, 86.3 crew-hours) — more as a total than the two-story colonial, because scrape and primer hours live on every square foot, not in a published per-house adder. A 2-story 3,400 sf peeling masonry / elastomeric job with scrape, primer, eight shutters, occupied protection, and hard access prices about $15,585 (163.1 hours, $4.58 per square foot). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine on the ranch turns into a loss after the first extra story.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $36/h painter loaded at 32% payroll burden is $47.52. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. On the sample rates the brochure ranch walk-away is $1,397, so a $3,999 coupon still covers that house. The same coupon on the colonial does not. Replace every rate with your paint invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a lead-paint determination, a building-code inspection, a warranty that any surface will last a stated number of years, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Elevation square footage, stories, scrape condition, and whether a primer coat is required are yours to confirm.

Price your next job

Common questions

How much to charge to paint the exterior of a house?

Charge from the included one-story ranch, extra stories over that include, extra elevation square footage over the included ranch, extra trim, shutters, a scrape of failing paint, a primer coat, occupied-home protection, hard second-story access, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 1-story 1,800 sf two-coat ranch at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $1,940 — about $1.08 per elevation square foot.

Why is a flat $3,999 house special dangerous?

Homeowners count 'a house is a house.' Extra stories, extra elevation, extra trim, peeling paint, primer, shutters, and hard access do not live in a $3,999 coupon. The special can look fine on a ranch and still lose more than $500 on a two-story colonial.

Does a larger house always cost more per square foot?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates a 2-story 2,800 sf colonial with extra trim, twelve shutters, occupied protection, and hard access prices around $6,287 ($2.25 per elevation square foot), while a 1,800 sf one-story ranch prices around $1,940 ($1.08 per square foot).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not construction, painting, lead-paint, building-code, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

      Common questions

      What does this exterior paint estimate include?

      Base setup, extra hours for elevation and stories beyond your included allowance, a scrape and prime pass if you flag them, trim beyond the included footage, shutters, occupied-home protection, hard-access time, paint, primer, and caulk from your coverage and coat count, travel and equipment, and overhead and margin on top.

      What’s the difference between this and a flat house-special price?

      A flat price treats every house as the same job. This tool splits out a base allowance for elevation, stories, and trim from what goes beyond it, so a two-story colonial with extra trim, a scrape-and-prime pass, and hard second-story access prices differently than a one-story ranch with sound existing paint, instead of both landing on one number.

      Does changing the job type overwrite my own hourly rates?

      No. Picking a job type only suggests a starting setup time, paint cost per gallon, and coat count, and it will not replace a rate you have already typed over that suggestion. Every hour and dollar figure stays something you can edit.

      Does this cover interior painting or cabinet refinishing?

      No, this prices an exterior paint job specifically: elevation, stories, scrape and prime, and trim. Interior rooms and cabinet doors are a different scope with their own labor and material patterns and are not part of this calculation.

      Does it check for lead paint or the condition of the existing paint?

      No. Scrape and prime are flags you set from your own inspection, and the tool does not test for lead paint, assess paint condition, or perform any building-code check. Confirm those separately before starting work, especially on an older home.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us; your business and contact details for the printed proposal are saved locally on this device, and job numbers are not otherwise kept between visits.

vs-a-flat-3999-house-special.html.text:
← Exterior Painting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $3,999 house special

"$3,999 whole-house exterior paint" is not a price for a house — it is a price for one specific house, quietly applied to every house that calls for a quote.

What a flat house special is

A flat special is the fastest number a company can put on a postcard or a search ad: one price, no takeoff, easy for a homeowner to compare between bids. It works for the shop as a lead magnet and works for the homeowner as a round number to shop around with. Nothing about the number says which house it was built for.

The number was set for one job — commonly a smaller, one-story house with sound existing paint, standard trim, no scrape, no shutters, and easy ground-level access — and then quoted to every caller afterward, whether or not the next house looks anything like the one the special was priced on.

What this calculator does instead

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the house's elevation square footage, story count, trim length, shutters, and flags for scrape, primer, an occupied yard, and hard second-story access, plus your crew's wage, payroll burden, and target margin. It turns that into the crew hours the job actually consumes, the price per elevation square foot, and a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this house, not the house the special was built on.

What a flat house special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same price whether the house is a one-story 1,800 sq ft ranch with sound paint or a two-story 2,800 sq ft colonial with 240 lf of extra trim, shutters, an occupied yard, and hard access. Prices extra elevation square feet, extra stories, and extra trim as their own hour lines, so a bigger, harder house returns a bigger number instead of the same one.
Has no line for a scrape-and-prime pass, an occupied home needing extra protection, or hard second-story access — a peeling two-story colonial prices the same as a fresh one-story ranch. Adds scrape hours, primer coats and paint, occupied-home hours, and hard-access hours only when that scope is turned on, so peeling paint and hard access show up in the price instead of being absorbed into it.
Was priced once, on one house, and never re-derived from a scrape, an extra story, or a shutter count — it is a marketing number, not a cost-basis number. Recomputes crew hours, paint gallons, primer, and caulk from the exact scope entered every time, so the price tracks the job rather than a memory of the postcard rate.
On this calculator's own 2-story, 2,800 sq ft colonial preset with extra trim, shutters, an occupied yard, and hard access, a $3,999 special lands about $527.61 below the walk-away cost of paint, labor, and overhead alone — before any profit is counted. Returns a walk-away price of about $4,526.61 and a bid price of about $6,286.96 for that same colonial, at this tool's own shop-rate defaults and a 28% target margin.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price, the price per elevation square foot, and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one house it was priced on, and nothing about a postcard rate tells a shop or a homeowner when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat special skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $3,999 house special get exterior painting wrong?

Because the crew hours and paint a house needs come from its elevation square footage, story count, trim length, scrape/prime condition, shutters, occupancy, and access — not from being "a house." A one-story 1,800 sq ft ranch with sound existing paint and a two-story 2,800 sq ft colonial with 240 lf of extra trim, twelve shutters, an occupied yard, and hard second-story access are both "a house," and a flat special charges them the same number.

What job is the $3,999 number actually built around?

One specific job, usually the easiest one a company is willing to advertise: a smaller, one-story house with sound existing paint, standard trim, no scrape, no shutters, and easy ground-level access. It is a marketing price meant to get the phone to ring, not a number derived from any particular customer's elevation, stories, or access.

What happens when the real job is bigger than the special's job?

On this calculator's own 2-story, 2,800 sq ft colonial preset — extra trim, twelve shutters, an occupied yard, and hard second-story access, priced at this tool's own shop-rate defaults — the walk-away cost of paint, labor, and overhead alone comes to about $4,526.61, and the bid price at a 28% target margin is about $6,286.96. Matching a $3,999 special on that job is about $527.61 under the walk-away cost, before any profit is counted — the job loses money the day it is scheduled, not just when it runs long.

What happens when the real job is smaller than the special's job?

On this calculator's own 1-story, 1,800 sq ft ranch preset — sound paint, no scrape, no shutters, easy access — the same shop-rate defaults price the job at about $1,940.12, with a walk-away cost of about $1,396.89. A $3,999 special on that house is more than double what the job itself costs to deliver, which is not a defect in the special so much as a sign the number was never tied to any one house's scope in the first place.

Is a flat house special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of houses close to the one the special was built around — similar size, one story, sound paint, standard trim, easy access — a flat number can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard price does not know which band a given house is in and neither does the crew until the elevation, stories, and access are actually measured.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, paint prices, or what competitors advertise. It takes the wage, paint cost, and overhead you enter and turns them into a walk-away price for the elevation, stories, trim, and access you describe — the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat house special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest way to advertise that works until the house stops matching the one the special was priced on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $1,940.12, $1,396.89, $6,286.96, and $4,526.61 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on the two worked jobs built into its own preset list (open the calculator and pick "1-story ranch" or "2-story colonial" from Starting house to reproduce them), not a claim about any specific contractor's real costs or any specific company's advertised price.

vs-paintscout.html.text:
← Exterior Painting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. PaintScout

Two different shapes: PaintScout is an account-based platform for estimating, proposing, and following up on every job a painting company's sales team sells. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this exterior job cost, given its elevation, stories, and access, before you open a sales tool.

What each tool is for

PaintScout is estimating, proposal, and sales-follow-up software built specifically for painting contractors — it describes itself as dedicated solely to the needs of painting businesses, unlike general-trade estimating tools. Companies use it to standardize how every estimator on a sales team prices and presents a job from shared finish-system templates, send that estimate on as a branded proposal, automate the follow-up that turns a sent quote into a signed job, and track the pipeline across every job the company runs. It is sold on an ongoing, per-seat subscription, with a separate add-on commonly used for job and production tracking once work is sold. PaintScout's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — painting-specific estimating and proposal software, sold as a per-seat account — are stated, and no dollar amount for PaintScout appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what PaintScout does. It does not store a customer record, brand a proposal with a company's finish-system library, or automate a follow-up sequence across a sales team. It takes one house's elevation square footage, story count, trim length, shutters, and flags for scrape, primer, an occupied home, and hard second-story access, plus crew wage, payroll burden, and target margin, and turns that into the crew hours the job actually consumes, the price per elevation square foot, the bid price, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Is the price I'm about to send still above my walk-away cost?This calculator's compare-to-proposed-price check.
I need automated follow-up on every proposal I send and reporting across every job my company sells.PaintScout — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.

Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. PaintScout is used through a paid account.

Most painting companies get different value from each: PaintScout (or a comparable painting-specific platform) for standardizing estimates, proposals, and follow-up across a whole sales team as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on what one exterior job should cost from its elevation and access before a sales system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed proposal, an invoice, or a paint-condition inspection.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or PaintScout?

They do different jobs, and a painting company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. PaintScout is estimating, proposal, and sales-follow-up software built specifically for painting contractors, sold on an ongoing per-seat subscription with a separate add-on for job and production tracking. It is built to standardize how a whole sales team prices and presents jobs, track those proposals through follow-up, and report on the pipeline across every estimator and every job the company runs. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from a house's elevation square footage, story count, trim length, shutters, and flags for scrape, primer, an occupied home, and hard access, it turns that into the price per elevation square foot, the crew hours the job actually consumes, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before you have entered anything into a sales system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A company that already runs its whole sales pipeline through one system and needs every estimator quoting from the same templates is better served by PaintScout or a comparable painting-specific platform; a painter who wants an instant, private gut-check on what a job should cost from its elevation and access before opening a sales tool is in the right place here.
